questions.q: In the double-slit experiment with both slits open and particles sent through one at a time, what pattern builds up on the detector screen, and why is this surprising for classical bullet-like particles?
options: A completely uniform, featureless spread across the whole screen

An interference pattern of alternating bright and dark bands, even though each individual particle lands as a single localized dot — classical bullets fired one at a time through two slits would just produce two bands, not an interference pattern
No particles reach the screen at all when both slits are open
A single bright band directly behind one slit, because particles always pick the easier path
questions.explain: Even one particle at a time, over many trials, builds up alternating bright/dark interference bands — the signature of waves adding constructively and destructively. Classical bullets could not produce this; each would just go through one slit or the other and contribute to one of two simple bands.

questions.q: What happens to the interference pattern when a which-path detector determines which slit each particle actually went through, and what does this reveal?
options: The interference pattern gets stronger because now there is more information
The particles stop reaching the screen entirely

The interference pattern disappears and is replaced by a simple two-band pattern, revealing that it is specifically the existence of definite which-path information — not physical disturbance alone — that destroys interference
Nothing changes; the interference pattern is unaffected by which-path detection
questions.explain: Obtaining which-path information collapses the shared two-path amplitude into a definite single-path description, eliminating the interference and leaving the plain two-band pattern. This happens however gently the information is obtained, showing it's the existence of a definite path fact that matters, not mechanical disturbance.

questions.q: What did de Broglie actually propose, and how was it experimentally confirmed?
options: That electrons are physically split in half when passing through two slits; confirmed by the double-slit screen pattern

That every particle with momentum has an associated wavelength inversely related to its momentum; confirmed when electron beams fired at crystals produced diffraction patterns matching that relationship
That atoms can only exist at discrete energy levels; confirmed by atomic spectral lines
That light is made of particles; confirmed by the photoelectric effect
questions.explain: De Broglie proposed matter itself carries a wave character with wavelength tied to momentum. This was confirmed directly by electron diffraction off crystals, a classic wave phenomenon, with spacing matching his predicted relationship — not by the photoelectric effect or spectral lines, which are separate pieces of evidence from the previous lesson.

questions.q: Precisely stated, what does "wave-particle duality" mean according to this lesson?
options: A quantum object's amplitude spreads across multiple possibilities and interferes like a wave; a definite, localized, particle-like outcome appears only when a measurement forces one
A particle is simultaneously a fully-formed wave and a fully-formed particle at every instant, with no further explanation needed
Particles behave like waves only when scientists are not observing them, and like particles only when scientists are watching
Wave-particle duality is an outdated idea with no role in modern quantum mechanics
questions.explain: The precise statement separates the two behaviors: amplitude spread across possibilities produces wave-like interference, while measurement always yields one definite, localized, particle-like result. It is not a vague simultaneous-wave-and-particle claim, and it remains central to modern quantum mechanics.

questions.q: Why does the double-slit interference phenomenon matter for understanding how quantum algorithms work, beyond being a historical experiment?
options: Quantum algorithms rely on exactly this mechanism: amplitudes spread across multiple computational paths are engineered to interfere constructively for correct answers and destructively for wrong ones, before a final measurement forces one definite readout
It matters only because it inspired the name "quantum computing"
It matters only for building quantum hardware, not for designing algorithms
It doesn't matter — quantum algorithms use entirely different physics
questions.explain: A quantum algorithm's amplitudes across different computational paths are shaped so wrong answers cancel (destructive interference) and the right answer reinforces (constructive interference), then measurement collapses everything to one readout — the exact same amplitude-interference-then-collapse mechanism as the double-slit experiment.
